newsitem.title: USA: Orange County bankruptcy trial gets underway.
newsitem.headline: Orange County bankruptcy trial gets underway.

text.p: Orange County assistant treasurer Matthew Raabe concealed fund diversions and risky investments that led to the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history, prosecutors alleged on Monday.

Deputy Orange County District Attorney Matthew Anderson told a jury of six men and six women that Raabe was behind a scheme to divert interest earnings from local governments that had invested in the county-run portfolio.
"No, he didn't put it (the diverted funds) in his own pocket," Anderson said in his opening remarks. "But he put it in his employer's pocket. He gave it to the county of Orange."
Raabe's defense will deliver its opening remarks later on Monday. His attorneys are expected to say that Raabe followed the instructions of then-county treasurer Robert Citron.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
Raabe was indicted in May 1995 on several counts, including making false statements in the sale of securities and misappropriation of public funds.
Raabe, who has denied any wrongdoing, faces up to 12 years in prison. His trial could last until mid-May, attorneys said.
Raabe was one of several Orange County officials to face charges following the bankruptcy.

In April 1995, Citron pleaded guilty to six felonies for his role in the crisis. A judge last November ordered him to spend a year in jail and pay a $100,000 fine, but Citron was later assigned to a community work program instead of jail.
Citron's attorney claimed that his client was "manipulated" by Raabe, who allegedly was the "mastermind."
Last October, a judge sentenced former Orange County budget director Ronald Rubino to probation for charges stemming from the investment crisis.
The case against county auditor Steven Lewis was put on hold by a state court pending a decision on his motion to disqualify the district attorney.
The Orange County bankruptcy also prompted the Securities and Exchange Commission to take action.
In January 1996, the SEC filed complaints against Citron and Raabe for making "material misstatements and omissions" in the official statements for county bond issues.
